title: The Fear That Makes You Run Toward God, Not Away From Him
paragraphs: The Fear That Makes You Run Toward God, Not Away From Him
Understanding “The Fear of the Lord” Correctly—and why the God who should leave us trembling is the very God who invites sinners to come home.
There is a kind of fear that makes you hide.
And there is a kind of fear that makes you kneel.
Confuse the two, and you can spend years calling anxiety “holiness,” distance “reverence,” and terror “the fear of the Lord.”
Maybe that has been your story.
You heard someone say, “Fear God,” and somewhere deep inside, you translated it into something Scripture never actually said:
God is waiting for you to mess up.
So you became careful.
Not surrendered. Careful.

You prayed carefully. Worshiped carefully. Confessed carefully. You tried to keep your failures out of sight—as though the God who formed your inward parts could somehow be kept from seeing the rooms you refused to open.
Then you failed again.
And suddenly you were Adam among the trees.
“I was afraid… so I hid.”
That sentence from Genesis 3:10 still describes millions of people.
Afraid.
So hiding.
But what if the biblical “fear of the Lord” was never supposed to drive a repentant sinner deeper into hiding?
What if understanding it correctly could completely change the way you see holiness, grace, obedience, worship—and even your own failures?
Stay with this, because Scripture contains a sentence so startling that, at first glance, it almost sounds contradictory.
The Bible tells us to fear God.
Then the Bible tells us that with God there is forgiveness… so that He may be feared.
Yes.
Forgiveness produces fear.
That changes everything.
Psalm 130:3–4 says:
“If You, LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But there is forgiveness with You, that You may be feared.”
The Hebrew phrase translated “that You may be feared” is לְמַעַן תִּוָּרֵא — lemaʿan tivvareʾ, from the Hebrew root ירא — y-r-ʾ, associated with fear, reverence, and awe.
Notice the movement of the Psalm.
Sin.
Judgment.
Human helplessness.
Then forgiveness.
Then fear.
The psalmist does not say, “There is forgiveness with You, therefore nobody needs to take You seriously.”
He says almost the opposite.
There is forgiveness with You…
therefore You are feared.
Why?
Because biblical fear is far deeper than being frightened that God might hurt you.
It is the soul awakening to the unbearable weight of who God actually is.
Holy.
Sovereign.
Righteous.
Creator.
Judge.
Merciful.
Near.
The One against whom you have sinned is also the One who forgives you.
And when that truth finally gets beneath your religious vocabulary, something happens.
You stop treating grace cheaply.
Imagine standing guilty before a perfectly righteous Judge.
There is no excuse left.
No defense.
No comparison with someone worse than you.
No religious performance you can slide across the table.
The evidence is already there.
And the Judge is not corrupt.
He cannot simply pretend evil is good.
Then imagine discovering that the Judge Himself has provided the satisfaction of justice at unimaginable cost.
That is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because at the center of our faith is not humanity climbing toward God.
It is God coming toward sinners in Jesus Christ.
The cross does not tell us that sin was insignificant.
The cross tells us sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And simultaneously, the cross tells us that God's love toward sinners is so astonishing that Christ willingly gave Himself for us.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became respectable.
Not once our secret history became presentable.
While we were sinners.
This is where fear and grace meet.
The person who understands neither holiness nor grace can casually say, “God will forgive me.”
The person beginning to understand both falls silent and thinks:
He forgave even me?
That trembling is closer to the fear of the Lord.
Proverbs 1:7 declares:
יִרְאַת יְהוָה רֵאשִׁית דָּעַת
Yirʾat YHWH reʾshit daʿat.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.”
The expression יִרְאַת יְהוָה — yirʾat YHWH means “the fear of the LORD.”
This is not presented as an embarrassing stage of spiritual immaturity.
It is the beginning of knowledge.
Why?
Because wisdom begins when God becomes God in your understanding again.
Not your assistant.
Not your cosmic vending machine.
Not a motivational accessory attached to your ambitions.
Not a grandfatherly figure whose primary purpose is approving whatever you already wanted to do.
God.
When you begin seeing Him as He reveals Himself, your entire life is rearranged.
Your pride looks different.
Your secret sin looks different.
Your money looks different.
Your sexuality looks different.
Your grudges look different.
Your entertainment looks different.
Your ambitions look different.
Your words look different.
Your worship looks different.
And grace looks infinitely more beautiful.
This is why Proverbs 8:13 can say:
“The fear of the LORD is to hate evil.”
Real fear of God does not merely create religious feelings.
It changes allegiance.
You begin hating what destroys communion with the God you have come to treasure.
That does not mean a Christian instantly becomes sinless.
It means sin can no longer comfortably remain your unquestioned master.
There is a difference between falling into sin and building a home there.
There is a difference between struggling and surrendering.
There is a difference between temptation and making peace with rebellion.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly why those sentences hurt.
There is something you have been excusing.
Something hidden.
Something repeatedly renamed so you would not have to call it what Scripture calls it.
Maybe nobody knows.
But God does.
And strangely, that should not only terrify you.
For the person willing to repent, it should also give you hope.
Because the God who sees everything is the God before whom hiding is finally unnecessary.
You can confess what He already knows.
You can bring into the light what has been poisoning you in darkness.
You do not need to impress Jesus into saving you.
You need Jesus because you cannot save yourself.
This is why the fear of the Lord and the Gospel belong together.
At Sinai, God's holiness was not casual.
At Calvary, God's holiness did not disappear.
The cross is not God abandoning justice so He can become nice.
At the cross, we see both the horror of sin and the magnitude of divine mercy.
Jesus Christ, truly righteous, bore sin on behalf of sinners.
As 2 Corinthians 5:21 declares, God made the One who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
That is grace.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that does not wink at rebellion but rescues rebels.
Grace that does not say, “Remain exactly as you are.”
Grace says, “Come exactly as you are—and follow Christ.”
There is a difference.
Jesus receives sinners.
And Jesus transforms sinners.
That is why our theme will always be:
But notice who does the rewriting.
Jesus.
Not positive thinking.
Not religious image management.
Not self-improvement.
Jesus Christ.
Perhaps this is where you misunderstood fear.
You thought fearing God meant spending every waking moment wondering whether He was about to crush you.
Scripture gives us something richer.
Psalm 103:13 says:
“As a father pities his children, so the LORD pities those who fear Him.”
Read that again.
Those who fear Him receive fatherly compassion.
Psalm 147:11 likewise says that the LORD takes pleasure in those who fear Him, in those who hope in His mercy.
Fear.
Hope.
Mercy.
Together.
Biblical fear is not the opposite of trusting God.
Properly understood, it belongs alongside trust.
It recognizes God's terrifying majesty while resting in His covenant mercy.
It refuses to make God small enough to manage.
It refuses to make grace cheap enough to exploit.
It bows.
It listens.
It obeys.
It worships.
It repents.
And yet it draws near.
The New Testament preserves this same reality.
Hebrews 12:28–29 tells believers to serve God acceptably “with reverence and godly fear,” because “our God is a consuming fire.”
The Greek expression includes εὐλάβεια — eulabeia, carrying the sense of reverence or godly awe.
God did not stop being holy when Jesus came.
Jesus did not arrive to rescue humanity from an embarrassing Old Testament version of God.
The Father and the Son are not opponents.
The Gospel reveals the saving purpose of the triune God.
And here is where Hebrews becomes breathtaking.
The same letter that speaks about reverence and consuming fire also tells believers to approach God's throne boldly because of Christ.
Hebrews 4:16 invites us to come boldly to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace in time of need.
Do you see the beautiful tension?
He is a consuming fire.
Come near.
He is holy.
Come near.
He knows you completely.
Come near.
You need mercy.
Come near.
How?
Not arrogantly.
Not because sin does not matter.
Not because God lowered His standards.
We come through Jesus Christ.
The fear of the Lord does not make the redeemed person casually stroll into God's presence.
But neither does it leave that person outside the door.
It makes you enter with wonder.
There is another passage that helps protect us from misunderstanding.
First John 4:18 says:
“There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear involves torment.”
The Greek word commonly translated “fear” there is φόβος — phobos, while the passage specifically connects this fear with κόλασις — kolasis, punishment.
John is addressing fear connected with judgment and punishment.
So Scripture can tell believers both to fear God and that perfect love drives out fear because it is not using “fear” in a simplistic, identical sense in every context.
The child of God does not need to live as though Christ's finished work were meaningless and condemnation were still hanging over every forgiven failure.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation.
That is not permission to sin.
That is permission to stop pretending.
There are people who continue hiding because they think shame will make them holy.
It won't.
There are people punishing themselves for sins they have confessed because suffering somehow feels more spiritual than receiving forgiveness.
But your self-punishment cannot improve the blood of Jesus.
Repentance is necessary.
Obedience matters.
Holiness matters.
But salvation is not Christ plus your ability to hate yourself sufficiently.
The Gospel calls you away from both presumption and despair.
Presumption says, “God is loving, so my sin doesn't matter.”
Despair says, “My sin is so terrible that God's grace cannot reach me.”
The cross destroys both lies.
At Calvary, God says sin matters more than you imagined.
And grace reaches farther than you imagined.
That is the scandal.
Peter denied Jesus.
David committed grievous sin.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The woman caught in adultery was publicly humiliated.
The thief beside Jesus was dying under condemnation.
Scripture never sanitizes human failure to make its heroes marketable.
Because Scripture is ultimately not the story of impressive people rescuing themselves.
It is the story of a holy God redeeming sinners.
And perhaps that is why you are still reading.
Because somewhere underneath everything people see, you know there is a chapter of your story you wish you could tear out.
Maybe it happened years ago.
Maybe it happened yesterday.
Maybe it is happening right now.
Listen carefully.
Grace does not mean pretending the chapter was beautiful.
Grace means Jesus is capable of writing beyond it.
Repentance does not erase historical consequences.
Forgiveness does not always remove earthly consequences.
But your worst chapter does not have authority to become the final sentence when Christ takes hold of your life.
That is what fearing God correctly eventually does.
It makes sin frightening…
but God irresistible.
It makes rebellion bitter…
and mercy sweet.
It makes obedience something deeper than avoiding punishment.
You begin wanting to please the One who rescued you.
Think of Joseph when tempted by Potiphar's wife.
His question was not merely, “What happens if somebody catches me?”
He said, in Genesis 39:9:
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
That is fear of the Lord operating when nobody important is watching.
Human fear asks:
Will I get caught?
Fear of God asks:
How could I do this against Him?
Human fear protects reputation.
Fear of God protects communion.
Human fear performs when people are watching.
Fear of God remains when the door closes.
That distinction exposes us.
What do you watch when nobody knows?
What conversation would embarrass you if it became public?
What bitterness have you protected because forgiveness feels unfair?
What compromise have you renamed “weakness” even though you have stopped fighting it?
What does your private life say about how large God is in your heart?
Do not answer for somebody else.
This is between you and God.
And if something just surfaced in your conscience, do not run from Him.
Run toward Him.
Confess it.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Notice the language.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
The Gospel is not merely about being forgiven from something.
Christ is also transforming His people for something.
Holiness.
Love.
Truth.
Good works.
Worship.
Mission.
A life increasingly shaped by Jesus.
And that means the fear of the Lord is not meant to paralyze you.
It frees you from lesser fears.
When God becomes enormous in your sight, human approval begins shrinking.
You do not need everybody to clap.
You do not need everybody to understand.
You do not need everybody to approve your obedience.
Jesus said in Matthew 10:28 not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul, but rather to fear the One who has authority over both soul and body in hell.
Those are serious words.
Jesus Himself taught the judgment of God.
A Christ-centered message cannot erase judgment without erasing part of Christ's own teaching.
Hell is not a marketing device.
Judgment is not a preacher's prop.
Scripture treats final judgment as reality.
And precisely because eternity matters, the Gospel is extraordinarily urgent.
If you have never surrendered yourself to Jesus Christ, do not reduce this article to interesting Hebrew and Greek words.
You do not merely need a better definition of fear.
You need reconciliation with God.
Jesus calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Repentance is more than feeling bad.
It is a turning—a change of mind and direction that bears fruit in life.
Faith is more than admitting that Jesus existed.
It is entrusting yourself to Him.
His death.
His resurrection.
His lordship.
His mercy.
His righteousness rather than yours.
You may have spent years running because you were afraid of God.
But perhaps today you need to discover the fear that finally makes you stop running away.
The fear that whispers:
He is God.
I am not.
I have sinned.
He is holy.
Christ is merciful.
So I will come home.
And Christian, if you already belong to Christ but have grown casual with Him, perhaps you need this reminder too.
Grace should never make Jesus ordinary to you.
The more deeply you understand forgiveness, the more astonishing the Forgiver should become.
The hands pierced for you should never become boring.
The empty tomb should never become background decoration.
The name of Jesus should never become merely branding.
We are talking about the King.
The Lamb.
The Savior.
The One before whom every knee will ultimately bow.
And somehow, through His Gospel, sinners like us are invited near.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. Wisdom matters, and some confessions belong in private before God and with trustworthy mature believers rather than on a public page.
But you do not have to pretend anymore.

And if Christ has already delivered you from a season where shame once controlled you, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer desperately needed tonight.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy, but because there will probably be a day when shame tries to convince you to hide again.
Come back and remember:
The fear of the Lord does not make grace smaller.
It makes grace astonishing.
We want people receiving daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Your support can participate in the work of putting biblical encouragement in front of people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
Know Christ.
Fear God.
Turn from sin.
Receive grace.
Walk in obedience.
Love Him.
And never confuse being terrified of rejection with biblical reverence for the Father who receives His children through Christ.
Because perhaps the greatest surprise hidden inside “the fear of the Lord” is this:
When you finally understand how holy God is, you realize you should never have been able to approach Him.
Then you look at the cross…
and discover that Jesus opened the way.
The God before whom you should tremble is the God who, through Christ, tells the repentant sinner to come near.
